content: Eucalyptus globulus, commonly known as the Tasmanian Blue Gum, Southern Blue Gum, or Blue Gum Eucalyptus, is an evergreen tree that is native to Australia. It is one of the most widely cultivated tree species in the world. These trees typically grow to heights ranging from 30 to 55 meters (98 to 180 feet). The natural distribution of this species includes Tasmania and southern Victoria, with isolated populations found on King Island, Flinders Island in Bass Strait, and the summit of the You Yangs. The bark of the Tasmanian Blue Gum frequently sheds, peeling off in large strips. The juvenile leaves are broad and arranged in opposite pairs on square stems. These leaves measure approximately 6 to 15 cm in length and are covered with a blue-grey, waxy coating, which gives rise to the common name blue gum. The mature leaves are narrow, sickle-shaped, and dark green with a shiny surface. They are alternately arranged on rounded stems and can range from 15 to 35 cm in length. The flower buds of this species are top-shaped, ribbed, and warty, with a flattened operculum (a cap on the flower bud) that features a central knob. The cream-colored flowers are borne singly in the leaf axils and produce abundant nectar, which is used to create a strongly flavored honey. The flowers are approximately 5 cm in diameter. The fruit of the tree contains numerous small seeds, which are released through valves that open at the top of the fruit. The root system of the Tasmanian Blue Gum extends throughout the soil profile, penetrating several feet deep in some soil types. However, these trees do not develop taproots. On November 27, 1962, the Tasmanian Blue Gum was officially declared the floral emblem of Tasmania. The species name globulus is derived from the Latin word for little button, referring to the shape of the operculum. In Australia, the Blue Gum is the most commonly planted hardwood species, accounting for 65% of all plantation hardwoods in the country, with approximately 4,500 square kilometers of land dedicated to its cultivation. Most of these plantations are owned by international paper producers. The tree is also widely cultivated in other parts of the world for its timber and, in some cases, for the extraction of eucalyptus oil from its leaves. It was introduced to California in the mid-1800s and is now a prominent feature in many parks in San Francisco and throughout the state.
